newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti wants to speed move to telecoms.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti wants to speed move to telecoms.

text.p: Olivetti chief executive Francesco Caio was quoted as saying on Sunday the high-tech group would speed up a move into high-earning telecommunications without bailing out of all its traditional businesses.

Caio, interviewed in financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore, said the loss-making Italian group, whose chairman Carlo De Benedetti resigned suddenly last week, would not spin off its 41 percent-owned Omnitel mobile phone joint venture.

He said Olivetti had plans to integrate its businesses with the world of telecoms as part of "a strategy which wants to reposition the group without reneging on its past by synthesising it with the developments of the market."

"To understand Olivetti's strong and weak points it means making choices on the activities the company can do best and abandoning ambitions in business in which it can't find space, so concentrating resources where they are useful," he said.

Asked if this included the loss-making personal computer operation, which has been a major drag on the group in the competitive climate of the 1990s, Caio replied that Olivetti's products were competitive in that area.
"But the question is really another one -- can we become a leader? And the answer is no," he said.
In that case the company needed to find a solution "which permits us to focus resources where we have decided to expand, safeguarding the value of our activities in this sector."
He declined to say whether Olivetti was seeking a partner to whom it might sell all or part of Olivetti Personal Computers, adding "We are working to find the best solution."
Some industry watchers say Olivetti should get out of PCs before it drags down the entire group.

The past week has been traumatic for Olivetti, with De Benedetti, at the helm for nearly two decades, resigning suddenly as the company announced it had clocked up yet another loss for the first half of 1996, after five years in the red.

The group's shares were suspended in Milan on Thursday and Friday as stock market regulator Consob sought clarification of comments by a former top manager that its half year announcement did not represent the true state of its finances.

Olivetti said late on Friday its first half results, showing a pre-tax loss of 440.2 billion lire ($291 million) and net debt of 1.261 trillion lire, were drawn up in strict observation of current legal standards and accounting practices.

The stock is due to resume trade on Monday but Consob said it had so far had little time to study the financial details and wanted to make further investigations, including talking to the group's internal auditors.

Newspapers said Consob sources said it was also making a "routine" check into the excessive movement in the last few days of the group's shares, which fell some nine percent before news of the loss and De Benedetti's resignation last Tuesday.
They also said while Olivetti ordinary shares were suspended at 749 lire on Thursday, a packet of shares had changed hands at 650 lire on London's unofficial grey market on Friday.

Caio, admitting the damage to the group from the last few days had been enormous, told Il Sole he was flying to London on Monday to meet clients and understand their needs, saying: "Situations like the one we are facing aren't overcome in one or two days with a wave of a magic wand."
At a forum at this lakeside resort, business leaders were sanguine about the crisis at one of the country's most prominent companies, saying Olivetti had the tools to soldier on.
But Giorgio Fossa, chairman of employers' association Confindustria, said the government should throw out suggestions floated by some politicians that it should rescue the company.
"We cannot think of putting Olivetti on the shoulders of the state," he said.
